taxa.note: The fly agaric this region actually has: peach to melon-orange rather than scarlet, often fading to nearly cream at the margin, with pale warts that wash off in rain. The base is bulbous with rings of scales rather than a bag, which is the character that separates the whole group from the deadly white ones.

lookalikes.note: The yellow-orange fly agaric of the north is lemon to egg-yolk; this is peach to melon. They are the same mushroom in every other respect and the line between them is geography as much as colour.

taxa.note: A big pale parasol on lawns and playing fields, often in rings and arcs. The gills stay white for days and then turn dull green, and the print is green — no other large parasol here does that. It is the commonest cause of mushroom poisoning in North America, and the reason is simply that it grows where people walk. Wait for the print.

taxa.note: A hard, thick-skinned ball on the ground, ochre and coarsely scaly. Cut it: it is solid and purple-black inside almost from the start, where a puffball of the same size is uniform white paste. That cut is the whole of telling them apart.

lookalikes.note: Cut it in half. The inside here is hard and purple-black to purple-grey even when young; an edible puffball is pure white and soft. The rind is 1–3 mm thick and tough, not paper thin.

sources: MushroomExpert.com (Michael Kuo) - facts only, not redistributed text

taxa.note: A hard pale ball half buried in bare or trodden ground, which splits open from the top into a coarse star as it matures. Thick rind, and black-purple spore mass inside almost from the start — a puffball is white paste throughout at the size you would want to pick one.

season.note: Late summer through winter on hard ground.

lookalikes.note: A puffball is white and uniform inside while it is worth anything. This has a thick rind and is dark inside almost at once.

taxa.note: Small tan-orange brackets fused edge to edge in dense sheets along fallen hardwood branches, often running for a foot or more. Smooth underneath like the other parchments, and crowded together in a way the larger ones are not.

season.note: Recorded here in every month: it persists rather than fruits and passes.

lookalikes.note: Turkey tail has pores underneath. This is smooth, and much smaller.

taxa.note: Turn it over. Turkey tail has a white surface finely pitted with pores you can see with a lens; this is smooth underneath, with nothing to see at all. The top is banded in much the same browns and tans, so the top will not settle it and the underside settles it at once.

season.note: A bracket that persists, and recorded here in every month.

lookalikes.note: Turkey tail has pores underneath and this has a smooth surface. Both are banded on top and that band is no help.

lookalikes.note: Chicken-fat suillus is small, slimy, yellow and tied to white pine, often with a ring zone. Porcini is dry, brown and heavy.

taxa.note: A bolete shaggy with dark red fibres over a yellow ground, with a ring and yellow pores that stain brown where pressed. It goes with white pine and very little else, so the tree is half the identification.

season.note: Through the summer under white pine, heaviest in August.

taxa.note: A tough banded bracket whose underside is folded into blades running out from the attachment, so it looks gilled and is not. The blades are part of the same leathery flesh and will not come away as a gill does.

season.note: A bracket that persists, and recorded here in every month.

lookalikes.note: Turkey tail has fine pores; this has blades wide enough to count. Otherwise they are the same banded bracket on the same dead hardwood.

lookalikes.note: Both are small zoned brackets on fallen hardwood. This one is white and sits on a cup it grew from; turkey tail is banded in colour and has no cup.

lookalikes.note: The parchments make thin brackets with a free edge. This is flat against the wood and cracked into tiles.
